html: The cerebral cortex is the brain’s largest and most expansive learning substrate. In the human brain, approximately 16-20 billion neurons are distributed across a roughly 2000cm22000\,cm^2 sheet (often reported in the ∼2000\sim 2000-2500cm22500\,cm^2 range depending on method), folded into gyri and sulci yet remarkably uniform in its basic circuit motifs 1, 2, 3, 4. As detailed in the "Whole-Brain Architecture" section, this sheet is organized into a hierarchy of areas–e.g., 180 per hemisphere in the HCP multimodal parcellation 5–interconnected by a dense web of white-matter projections whose aggregate wiring length dwarfs that of any other brain structure. Here we revisit this architecture only to the extent needed to frame the cortex’s central learning problem: how does a recurrent, hierarchical, massively parallel network generate, propagate, and exploit error signals to build increasingly accurate generative models of the world?
